question: to the Commission Ilhan Kyuchyuk (Renew) Subject:

The continued Russian aggression against Ukraine and the EU’s sanctions regime targeting the Russian Federation, particularly in the energy sector, have fundamentally reshaped the EU’s energy landscape. At the same time, the escalating conflict in the Middle East and the disruption of maritime traffic through the Strait of Hormuz are exerting additional pressure on global energy markets, further exposing the EU’s structural vulnerabilities and external dependencies. These overlapping crises raise critical questions regarding the adequacy, pace and coherence of the EU’s energy transition and security policies. In the light of the above: 1.

Does the Commission envisage an accelerated and comprehensive strategy for achieving strategic autonomy in the field of energy, including a decisive diversification of supply sources and routes and a substantial scaling-up of domestic energy production capacities within the EU?

To what extent is the Commission considering a recalibration of existing policy frameworks, including the European Green Deal, in order to better reflect current geopolitical realities while ensuring energy security, affordability and industrial competitiveness?

Is the Commission prepared to adopt a more technologically neutral approach by reassessing the role of shale gas, nuclear energy and, where necessary, the temporary reactivation or extension of coal-based energy capacities, as part of a pragmatic and resilient energy mix during periods of acute external disruption?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (12.6.2026) The Commission is committed to strengthening the EU’s energy independence. The energy transition is an opportunity for the EU to reduce dependence on fossil fuel imports, shifting to homegrown energy sources. With REPowerEU1, the EU committed to end Russian fossil fuel dependency. In addition, the actions set out in AccelerateEU will help shelter EU citizens and industries from volatile global energy markets. The crisis in the Middle East highlighted once more that Europe’s dependency on fossil fuel imports creates vulnerability that comes at a price. It clearly confirms that long-term affordability depends on accelerating the clean energy transition. Scaling up domestic clean energy and energy efficiency will reduce fossil fuel imports and strengthen industrial competitiveness. The upcoming Electrification Action Plan will lay out concrete actions that serve these goals together with actions on heating and cooling and geothermal energy. The EU’s approach to technology neutrality in the energy sector is guided by the principle of allowing the market to determine the least-cost solution to achieve policy goals to achieve climate neutrality by 20502. This principle is underpinned by the right of Member States to choose their energy mix, as per Article 194 (2) of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union.
1 COM(2022) 230 final and Regulation (EU) 2026/261. 2 As set out in the European Climate Law (Regulation (EU) 2021/119) and governed by the Governance
